title: Exercise Science
front: Q100. Sliding filament sequence: excitation
back: Excitation 1. An action potential occurs in an alpha motor neuron axon. 2. ACh is released by the axon terminal of the alpha motor neuron at the neuromuscular junction. 3. Nicotinic receptor channels in the sarcolemma open, and the postsynaptic sarcolemma depolarizes (EPSP). 4. Voltage-gated sodium channels in the sarcolemma open and an action potential is generated in the muscle fiber, which sweeps down the sarcolemma and into the T tubules. 5. Depolarization of the T tubules causes Ca 2 release from the SR.

title: Exercise Science
front: Q101. Sliding filament sequence: contraction
back: Contraction 1. Ca 2 binds to troponin. 2. Tropomyosin shifts position and myosin binding sites on actin are exposed. 3. Myosin heads bind actin. 4. Myosin heads pivot. 5. An ATP binds to each myosin head and it disengages from actin. 6. The cycle continues as long as Ca 2 and ATP are present.

title: Exercise Science
front: Q102. Sliding filament sequence: relaxation
back: Relaxation 1. As EPSPs end, the sarcolemma and T tubules return to their resting potentials. 2. Ca 2 is sequestered by the SR by an ATP-driven pump. 3. Myosin binding sites on actin are covered by tropomyosin.

back: All type 1 motor units are activated before any type 2. (All-or-none is a separate principle.)

back: A band (length of myosin). The I band and H zone shorten during a concentric contraction.

back: Autogenic inhibition - Golgi tendon organ senses high tension and signals the muscle to relax.

title: Exercise Science

back: Increased red blood cells (and it decreases plasma volume), raising hematocrit.

back: Type 2x to type 2a (more fatigue-resistant).

back: Decreased resting HR (larger LV/stroke volume); max HR unchanged by training.

back: Senses tension and inhibits the agonist muscle (located in the tendon).

title: Exercise Science
front: Q276. Which is a catabolic hormone: IGF-1, epinephrine, or growth hormone?
back: Epinephrine - a catecholamine that mobilizes/breaks down fuel sources.

title: Exercise Science
front: Q277. Which is NOT a rotator cuff muscle: supraspinatus, teres major, subscapularis?

title: Exercise Science
front: Q278. Which molecule CANNOT undergo gluconeogenesis: lactate, ATP, or amino acids?
back: ATP. Lactate, pyruvate, amino acids, and glycerol can; liver is the major site.

title: Exercise Science

back: Increased myoglobin content. (Submax HR decreases; LV wall thickness is a resistance adaptation.)

title: Exercise Science

back: Alveoli and capillaries (smallest-level vessels).

title: Exercise Science

back: Send full action potentials more rapidly (rate coding). Action potentials are all-or-none.

title: Exercise Science

back: Calcium binds troponin (not troponin binding actin); this moves tropomyosin off actin's binding sites.

title: Exercise Science
front: Q283. Which is a major catabolic effect of cortisol in muscle?
back: Converts amino acids to carbohydrates (glucose) and inhibits protein synthesis; increases proteolytic enzymes.

title: Exercise Science
front: Q284. During AEROBIC exercise, what happens to diastolic BP (and how does resistance training differ)?
back: AEROBIC: diastolic stays about the same or slightly drops (working-muscle vasodilation lowers peripheral resistance) while systolic rises. title: Exercise Science
front: Q285. Which process occurs OUTSIDE the mitochondria: glycolysis, Krebs, oxidative phosphorylation?
back: Glycolysis (splits glucose to pyruvate in the cytosol).

back: ~30% anaerobic / ~70% aerobic.

title: Exercise Science
front: Q287. Which is NOT a primary factor in EPOC?
back: Post-exercise peripheral vasoconstriction. (ATP/PCr resynthesis and O2 replenishment are factors.)

title: Exercise Science
front: Q288. Which hormone would you expect to DECREASE during exercise?
back: Insulin (exercise mobilizes glucose; cortisol and systolic BP rise).

title: Exercise Science
front: Q289. Which hormone has the GREATEST delay in release after intense resistance training?
back: IGF-1. (Testosterone peaks during/right after, then GH, then delayed IGF-1.)

title: Exercise Science
front: Q290. What is a function of IGF-1?
back: Protein anabolism (building muscle protein); it inhibits proteolytic enzymes.

back: Nordic hamstring curl. (Skull crusher triceps act as a 1st-class lever.)

back: Distal (farther from the body's center).

back: Both lipolysis (frees fatty acids) and beta oxidation (to acetyl-CoA -> Krebs).

title: Exercise Science
front: Q294. What is true about type 2a/2x fibers (re: motor unit grouping)?
back: By the size principle, type 1 motor units are recruited before type 2. Fibers of different motor units are intermingled in a pseudo-random MOSAIC within a fascicle - NOT segregated by type (perimysium wraps a whole fascicle, which holds many mixed motor units).

title: Exercise Science
front: Q295. During which gait phase does the psoas major contract concentrically?
back: Swing phase (hip flexion, swinging the leg forward).

title: Exercise Science
front: Q296. Approx EPOC (afterburn) from a 400-calorie HIIT workout?
back: ~40-60 extra calories (~10-15% of the session's calories).

title: Exercise Science

back: Gluteus medius (prevents hip drop and knee valgus on landing).

title: Exercise Science
front: Q298. Why do older athletes lose power before strength or endurance?
back: Type 2 muscle fiber denervation/atrophy (largest, high-threshold fibers).

front: Q299. Which aerobic training is done AT the lactate threshold?
back: Pace/tempo (threshold) training - ~race pace, ~20-30 min.

back: Economy (exercise/running economy). MET = O2 demand; VO2 = oxygen consumed.

back: Rate of force development. (Impulse = force x time; tendon stiffness also helps.)

title: Exercise Science

back: Increased mitochondrial density (and stroke volume; submax HR and resistance-driven hypertrophy decrease).

front: Q304. Energy system and work:rest for 30-second sprint repeats?
back: Anaerobic glycolysis, 1:4 (1:3-1:5 range).

back: ~2 minutes (anaerobic glycolysis 1:3-1:5 -> 75-125 s).

back: 1 min 45 s (fast glycolysis 1:3-1:5 -> 72-120 s).

title: Exercise Science

back: None of strength/power/sprint speed - specificity principle.

back: Muscle hypertrophy. (Early large gains are neuromuscular.)

back: Soccer throw-in (sagittal). Backhand/pitch involve transverse rotation.

back: Q = stroke volume x heart rate.

back: ~40-50% of VO2max.

back: 3.5 mL O2 per kg per minute.

back: 4-14% if under 4 weeks; 6-20% if over 4 weeks.

back: ~12 years old (females), ~14 years old (males).

back: ~1-1.5% per year.

back: Osteopenia: -1 to -2.5 SD; osteoporosis: below -2.5 SD.

back: GAS (general adaptation syndrome), Stimulus-Fatigue-Recovery-Adaptation, Fitness-Fatigue.

front: Q054. Anabolic steroids
back: Synthetic derivatives of testosterone

title: Nutrition
front: Q055. Precursors of hormones
back: Prohormones

title: Nutrition
front: Q056. Blood doping methods
back: Transfusion; erythropoietin (EPO)

title: Nutrition
front: Q057. Two types of performance enhancers
back: Hormone (and mimics); dietary supplements

title: Nutrition
front: Q058. Beta blockers
back: Block beta adrenergic receptors (ie catecholamine receptors); reduce anxiety and tremors

title: Nutrition
front: Q059. Beta agonist v beta blocker
back: Agonist is like epinephrine, inc HR, relax airway muscles; blocker opposite

title: Nutrition
front: Q060. Erythropoietin (EPO) adverse
back: Unregulated red blood cell production, increases viscosity

title: Nutrition
front: Q061. Anabolic steroid adverse effects
back: Acne, hair loss, roid rage, decrease sperm count

title: Nutrition
front: Q062. Loss of electrolytes leads to…
back: Reduced energy production, endurance

title: Nutrition
front: Q063. RMR using cunningham
back: RMR = 500 + 22 × (fat-free mass in kg). FFM = lean body mass; then × activity factor (1.2 sedentary-1.9 heavy) for total daily energy needs.

title: Nutrition
front: Q064. Low calorie diet, protein…
back: Needs to be higher like 1.8-2.7

title: Nutrition
front: Q065. Ideal drink for 2h aerobics

title: Nutrition
front: Q066. Sodium per liter to replace electrolytes

title: Nutrition
front: Q067. Balanced diet % protein, carb, fat

title: Nutrition
front: Q068. Eating disorders producing overweight, persistently under, cycling
back: Binge eating, anorexia, bulimia

title: Nutrition
front: Q069. Protein per kg for lean mass gain

title: Nutrition
front: Q070. Fiber DRI women v men
back: Fiber DRI: 21-25 g/day women, 30-38 g/day men

title: Nutrition
front: Q071. Most prevalent nutrition deficiency
back: Iron

title: Nutrition
front: Q072. Avoid losing more than __% of body weight (due to sweat) during exercise

title: Nutrition
front: Q073. Aerobic endurance should consume ___  multi carbs per hour

title: Nutrition
front: Q074. Best food ~1 hour before competition?
back: 8 oz sports drink + small banana (~8 oz fluid, ~35 g carbs - digestible in 1 hr).

title: Nutrition
front: Q075. When should a pregame meal with 115g carb / 20g protein / 3g fat be eaten?
back: 4-6 hours before competition (larger meals with protein/fat need more time).

title: Nutrition
front: Q076. Fluid/carb recommendation every 15 min during a marathon?
back: 3-8 oz liquid and ~10-15 g carbohydrate (about 1 g carb/min).

title: Nutrition
front: Q077. Athlete eats 98g fat on 2,900 kcal/day at stable weight - adjust fat?
back: Maintain. 98 x 9 = 882 kcal = ~30% of intake, within the 25-35% range.

title: Nutrition
front: Q078. 63kg XC runner ate 472g carb day before a race and felt flat - recommendation?
back: Increase carbs. Carb load 10-12 g/kg the 2 days prior; he needs at least ~630 g.

title: Nutrition
front: Q079. Which non-essential amino acid supplement improves anaerobic threshold but not aerobic power?
back: Beta-alanine (helps repeated high-effort work near anaerobic threshold).

title: Nutrition
front: Q080. How long does resistance training raise muscle sensitivity to amino acids?
back: 24-48 hours (anabolic effect of a single meal lasts ~3-5 hours).

title: Nutrition
front: Q081. Which post-exercise meal would NOT significantly replenish glycogen?
back: Chicken, 2 eggs, water, green beans - very low carbohydrate.

title: Nutrition
front: Q082. Which mineral deficiency progresses in 3 stages (depletion, marginal deficiency, anemia)?
back: Iron - most prevalent nutritional deficiency; causes weakness, fatigue, irritability.

title: Nutrition
front: Q083. Recommended daily protein for a strength/speed athlete?
back: 1.4-1.7 g/kg/day (endurance ~1.0-1.6; RDA 0.8).

title: Nutrition
front: Q084. What percent of calories from fat: 90g fat, 290g carb, 125g protein?
back: 33%. Fat 810 kcal / total 2470 kcal = ~33% (fat 9 kcal/g, carb/protein 4 kcal/g).

title: Nutrition
front: Q085. How long for muscle glycogen to recover?
back: ~24 hours.

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q001. Inverted-U hypothesis?
back: Performance rises with arousal to an optimal point, then declines as arousal gets too high.

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q002. Cognitive vs somatic anxiety?
back: Cognitive = mental (worry, negative thoughts). Somatic = physical (↑ HR, sweating, tension).

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q003. Self-determination: intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation?
back: Intrinsic = internal enjoyment/satisfaction (more durable). Extrinsic = external rewards (medals, money).

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q004. Process vs outcome goals?
back: Process = controllable actions/technique (best for performance). Outcome = winning/result (less controllable).

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q005. IZOF model?
back: Individual Zone of Optimal Functioning - each athlete has their own optimal arousal/anxiety band.

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q006. Arousal
back: the intensity of motivation at any given moment (or alertness)

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q007. Anxiety
back: Anxiety is a subcategory of arousal in that it is a negatively perceived emotional state characterized by nervousness, worry, apprehension, or fear and is associated with a physiological activation of the body

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q008. State v trait anxiety
back: State anxiety is the actual experience of apprehension and uncontrolled arousal. Trait anxiety is a personality characteristic, which represents a latent disposition to perceive situations as threatening.

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q009. Stress
back: Stress is defined as a substantial imbalance between demand (physical, psychological, or both) and response capability, under conditions in which failure to meet that demand has important consequences

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q010. Motivation
back: Motivation can be defined as the intensity and direction of effort (or impetus for goal directed behavior)

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q011. Distress
back: Negative stress, arousal but also anxiety

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q012. Opposite of distress
back: Eustress

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q013. Hull’s drive theory + when it fails
back: More arousal means more performance; but not for complex skills or less experience - too much arousal can be catastrophic

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q014. Inverted U theory
back: Arousal facilitates performance up to an optimal level, then reduces

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q015. Reversal theory
back: High levels of arousal may be scary and worrisome for one, exciting for another → you can reverse your interpretation

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q016. Achievement motivation
back: Effort to master a task, achieve excellence, win

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q017. Self controlled practice
back: Athlete decides practice structure; is asked how the believe they are going

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q018. Positive/negative reinforcement/punishment
back: Add/remove reward; inc/decrease (repeat/prevent) behavior

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q019. Selective attention
back: Suppression of task-irrelevant stimuli or thoughts

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q020. Nideffer attentional styles
back: Broad/narrow; internal/external

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q021. Diaphragmatic breathing
back: Deep breath + stomach protrusion to lower diaphragm

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q022. Self confidence v self efficacy
back: Self-confidence is the belief that one can successfully perform a desired behavior (40), while self-efficacy, a situationally specific form of self-confidence, is the perception of one’s ability to perform a given task in a specific situation

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q023. How does limited skill change optimal arousal level
back: Decreases

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q024. Pure part, progressive part, repetitive part training

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q025. Variable v random practice
back: Variable is same skill with variation

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q026. MAF
back: Motive to avoid failure - not avoiding failure but avoiding perceived shame

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q027. Use of imagery
back: Start static, build to successful execution of a skill

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q028. Segmentation v fractionalization
back: S is where there are clear breaks; F is sub components that are simultaneous eg arms and legs in push press

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q029. Types of feedback
back: Intrinsic, augmented which has two subtypes knowledge of results, knowledge of performance (here means movement pattern)

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q030. One major response to injury other than depression
back: Alterations of appetite eg don’t deserve to eat

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q031. 3 phases of learning
back: Cognitive (declarative), associative (procedural), autonomous

title: Sport Psychology
front: Q032. Give an example of positive punishment.
back: Adding a mile run to decrease texting at practice (add a stimulus to reduce a behavior).

title: Program Design
front: Q001. %1RM for ~10 reps? (and 8/6/4?)

title: Program Design
front: Q002. Strength rep/intensity zone?
back: ≥85% 1RM, ≤6 reps

title: Program Design
front: Q003. Hypertrophy zone?

title: Program Design
front: Q004. Muscular endurance zone?

title: Program Design
front: Q005. RPE = ?
back: 10 − reps in reserve (RPE 8 = 2 RIR)

title: Program Design
front: Q006. Periodization order across a macrocycle?
back: Hypertrophy → strength → power → peaking (power is transient - train nearest competition)

title: Program Design
front: Q007. Karvonen formula?
back: Target HR = RHR + (intensity × [HRmax − RHR])

title: Program Design
front: Q008. Rest periods by goal?
back: Strength/power 2-5 min · Hypertrophy 30 s-1.5 min · Muscular endurance ≤30 s.

title: Program Design
front: Q009. Exercise order rule?
back: Power/explosive first → large multi-joint → small single-joint last.

title: Program Design
front: Q010. 2-for-2 rule?
back: If the athlete gets 2 extra reps on the last set in 2 consecutive sessions → increase the load.

title: Program Design
front: Q011. Linear vs undulating (DUP) periodization?
back: Linear: volume ↓ / intensity ↑ gradually over the macrocycle. Undulating: volume & intensity vary within the week.

title: Program Design
front: Q012. Plyometric frequency / recovery?
back: 48-72 hr between plyometric sessions.

title: Program Design
front: Q013. Taper - cut what, keep what?
back: Reduce VOLUME (~60-90%), MAINTAIN intensity → peak/supercompensation.

title: Program Design
front: Q014. Sprint speed = ?
back: Stride frequency × stride length. Acceleration = forward lean; max-velocity = upright posture.

title: Program Design
front: Q015. Sets by goal?
back: Strength 2-6 · Power 3-5 · Hypertrophy 3-6 · Muscular endurance 2-3.

title: Program Design
front: Q016. Plyometric volume (foot contacts) by level?
back: Beginner 80-100 · Intermediate 100-120 · Advanced 120-140 contacts.

title: Program Design
front: Q017. Depth jump box height?
back: Typically 30-32 in (range 16-42); avoid >42 in. Athletes >220 lb: avoid high-intensity / boxes >18 in.

title: Program Design
front: Q018. The 3 models of adaptation underlying periodization?
back: GAS (alarm→resistance→supercompensation→exhaustion); Stimulus-Fatigue-Recovery-Adaptation; Fitness-Fatigue paradigm.

title: Program Design
front: Q019. Periodization hierarchy (long→short)?
back: Macrocycle (~1 yr) → Mesocycle (2-6 wk) → Microcycle (~1 wk) → training session.

title: Program Design
front: Q020. Four periods of training?
back: Preparatory (off-season) → First Transition (pre) → Competitive (in-season) → Second Transition (active rest).

title: Program Design
front: Q021. Unloading / deload weeks - how often & how much?
back: Every 3-4 weeks, reduce total volume-load ~40-60%.

title: Program Design
front: Q022. Tapering before competition?
back: 7-28 days: reduce volume, KEEP intensity.

title: Program Design
front: Q023. Aerobic training types?
back: LSD (~70% VO₂max), Pace/Tempo (at LT), Interval (near VO₂max, 1:1), HIIT (>90%, 1:5), Fartlek (mixed).

title: Program Design
front: Q024. Resisted sprint loading limit?
back: Keep velocity loss ≤~10-12% (≈20-30% BW) so sprint mechanics stay intact.

title: Program Design
front: Q025. Training frequency by status?
back: Beginner 2-3/wk · Intermediate 3-4 · Advanced 4-7 (1-3 rest days per muscle group).

title: Program Design
front: Q026. Training frequency by season?
back: Off-season 4-6 · Pre-season 3-4 · In-season 1-3 · Post-season 0-3.

title: Program Design
front: Q027. Load-increase increments?
back: Smaller/weaker: +2.5-5 lb upper / +5-10 lower. Larger/stronger: +5-10 upper / +10-15 lower (≈2.5-10%).

title: Program Design
front: Q028. Core vs assistance exercise?
back: Core = multi-joint, large muscle groups (priority, sport transfer); assistance = single-joint, small muscle (balance/injury prevention).

title: Program Design
front: Q029. Structural vs power exercise?
back: Structural = loads the spine (trunk stabilization); power = a structural exercise done explosively (cleans, snatches).

title: Program Design
front: Q030. Plyometrics for youth?
back: Emphasize technique + supervision; avoid high-intensity & depth jumps; ≥2-3 days rest.

title: Program Design
front: Q031. Plyometrics for masters / older adults?
back: ≤5 low-moderate drills; longer recovery (3-4 days); avoid single-leg & depth jumps.

title: Program Design
front: Q032. Speed development progression?
back: Acceleration first (short, resisted/incline ≤20 m) → transition → max-velocity (fly-in sprints, 30-90 m).

title: Program Design
front: Q033. Cross-training - what it can and cannot do?
back: Maintains conditioning (must match duration + intensity) but cannot improve single-sport performance.

title: Program Design
front: Q034. Amortization phase?
back: Brief pause between eccentric & concentric of a plyometric - keep it SHORT (neural signaling to the agonist); too long = lost elastic/reflex benefit.

title: Program Design
front: Q035. List the seven program design variables in order.
back: Needs analysis, Exercise selection, Training frequency, Exercise order, Load and repetitions, Volume, Rest periods

title: Program Design
front: Q036. What are the two parts of a needs analysis?
back: Evaluation of the sport and assessment of the athlete

title: Program Design
front: Q037. List the three components of sport evaluation.
back: Movement analysis, Physiological analysis, Injury analysis

title: Program Design
front: Q038. List the three components of athlete assessment.
back: Training status and history, Testing and evaluation, Primary goal

title: Program Design
front: Q039. Define core exercises.
back: Multi joint exercises that involve large muscle areas and are priority for transfer to sport performance

title: Program Design
front: Q040. Define assistance exercises.
back: Single joint or small muscle group exercises used for injury prevention or balance

title: Program Design
front: Q041. Define structural exercises.
back: Exercises that load the spine and require trunk stabilization

title: Program Design
front: Q042. Define power exercises.
back: Structural exercises performed explosively such as cleans or snatches

title: Program Design
front: Q043. How many rest days should separate training for the same muscle group?
back: At least one and no more than three days

title: Program Design
front: Q044. Recommended training frequency per week for a beginner?
back: Two to three

title: Program Design
front: Q045. Recommended training frequency per week for an intermediate athlete?
back: Three to four

title: Program Design
front: Q046. Recommended training frequency per week for an advanced athlete?
back: Four to seven

title: Program Design
front: Q047. Typical training frequency for off season phase?
back: Four to six sessions per week

title: Program Design
front: Q048. Typical training frequency for preseason phase?
back: Three to four sessions per week

title: Program Design
front: Q049. Typical training frequency for in season phase?
back: One to three sessions per week

title: Program Design
front: Q050. Typical training frequency for postseason phase?
back: Zero to three sessions per week

title: Program Design
front: Q051. What is the standard exercise order?
back: Power exercises first then other core then assistance exercises

title: Program Design
front: Q052. Define a superset.
back: Two exercises performed back to back for opposing muscle groups

title: Program Design
front: Q053. Define a compound set.
back: Two exercises performed back to back for the same muscle group

title: Program Design
front: Q054. Define volume load.
back: Total weight lifted calculated as sets times reps times load

title: Program Design
front: Q055. Explain the repetition maximum continuum.
back: As percentage of one rep max decreases the number of possible repetitions increases

title: Program Design
front: Q056. Approximate number of reps at 75 percent 1RM.
back: Ten repetitions

title: Program Design
front: Q057. Approximate number of reps at 85 percent 1RM.
back: Six repetitions

title: Program Design
front: Q058. Approximate number of reps at 90 percent 1RM.
back: Four repetitions

title: Program Design
front: Q059. In what situation is one rep max testing appropriate?
back: For intermediate and advanced athletes with good technique

title: Program Design
front: Q060. Explain why power exercises use lighter percentages at the same repetition number.
back: To allow maximal velocity of movement rather than true repetition maximum effort

title: Program Design
front: Q061. State the two for two rule.
back: If two or more reps are completed over goal in the last set for two consecutive sessions increase load next time

title: Program Design
front: Q062. List typical load increases for smaller weaker athletes.
back: Upper body two point five to five pounds, Lower body five to ten pounds

title: Program Design
front: Q063. List typical load increases for larger stronger athletes.
back: Upper body five to ten pounds or more, Lower body ten to fifteen pounds or more

title: Program Design
front: Q064. List typical load increase range as a percent of load.
back: Two point five to ten percent

title: Program Design
front: Q065. Define repetition volume.
back: Total number of repetitions performed in a session

title: Program Design
front: Q066. Define average load per rep.
back: Volume load divided by total repetitions

title: Program Design
front: Q067. Typical set ranges by goal.
back: Strength two to six, Power three to five, Hypertrophy three to six, Endurance two to three

title: Program Design
front: Q068. Typical rest period for strength and power training.
back: Two to five minutes

title: Program Design
front: Q069. Typical rest period for hypertrophy training.
back: Thirty seconds to one and a half minutes

title: Program Design
front: Q070. Typical rest period for muscular endurance training.
back: Less than thirty seconds

title: Program Design
front: Q071. What are the primary programming goals for athletes training for power?
back: Maximize velocity and force output with appropriate recovery

title: Program Design
front: Q072. Define plyometric exercise.
back: Quick powerful movement using a pre stretch that activates the stretch shortening cycle to increase power

title: Program Design
front: Q073. What does SSC stand for?
back: Stretch Shortening Cycle

title: Program Design
front: Q074. List the three phases of the SSC.
back: Eccentric, Amortization, Concentric

title: Program Design
front: Q075. Describe the Mechanical model of plyometrics.
back: Elastic energy stored in the series elastic component during stretch and released during concentric action

title: Program Design
front: Q076. Describe the Neurophysiological model of plyometrics. (Neuro)
back: Muscle spindle stretch triggers reflex via Ia afferents to alpha motor neuron enhancing contraction

title: Program Design
front: Q077. What happens if the amortization phase is too long?
back: Stored energy dissipates and reflex contribution is lost

title: Program Design
front: Q078. Key coaching cue for force direction.
back: Push the ground away

title: Program Design
front: Q079. Why does a higher stretch rate increase concentric force? (Plyo)
back: Because it enhances elastic energy storage and reflex activation

title: Program Design
front: Q080. What are the main program design variables for plyometric training?
back: Warm Up, Needs analysis, Mode (exercise selection), Frequency, Intensity, Volume, Recovery/Rest, (Progression of F, I, V), Program Length

title: Program Design
front: Q081. List examples of lower body plyometric modes.
back: Jumps, hops, bounds, box drills, depth jumps

title: Program Design
front: Q082. List examples of upper body plyometric modes.
back: Medicine ball throws, plyometric push ups

title: Program Design
front: Q083. What determines plyometric intensity?
back: Stress on muscles connective tissue and joints affected by # contacts, speed, height and body weight

title: Program Design
front: Q084. How does intensity relate to volume?
back: As intensity increases volume should decrease

title: Program Design
front: Q085. Recommended plyometric frequency per week.
back: One to three sessions

title: Program Design
front: Q086. Recommended recovery between same region plyometric sessions.
back: Forty eight to seventy two hours

title: Program Design
front: Q087. Define a contact in plyometric volume measurement.
back: One foot strike or throw counted as a single repetition

title: Program Design
front: Q088. List the approximate plyometric volume recommendations by experience level.
back: Beginner 80-100, Intermediate 100-120, Advanced 120-200 contacts (low-intensity column)

title: Program Design
front: Q089. Typical plyometric program length.
back: Six to ten weeks

title: Program Design
front: Q090. List examples of dynamic warm up exercises before plyometrics.
back: Marching, skipping, lunges, footwork drills

title: Program Design
front: Q091. Criteria to start plyometric training.
back: Sufficient strength balance coordination and technical maturity

title: Program Design
front: Q092. What is the body mass limit and height for high intensity depth jumps?
back: Over two hundred twenty pounds should avoid heights above eighteen inches

title: Program Design
front: Q093. Recommended height range for depth jump boxes.
back: Sixteen to forty two inches with thirty to thirty two most common

title: Program Design
front: Q094. Describe adolescent plyometric guidelines.
back: Focus on technique and supervision, avoid high intensity or depth jumps, allow two to three days recovery

title: Program Design
front: Q095. Describe masters plyometric guidelines.
back: Limit to five or fewer low to moderate drills per session, allow three to four days recovery

title: Program Design
front: Q096. How should plyometrics integrate with resistance training?
back: Pair lower body plyo with upper body lifting and vice versa or alternate days

title: Program Design
front: Q097. What is complex training?
back: Combining heavy resistance exercise with plyometric movement to exploit post activation potentiation

title: Program Design
front: Q098. List examples of common plyometric drills by body region.
back: Lower body jumps hops bounds depth jumps, Upper body medicine ball throws push ups, Trunk modifications of core exercises

title: Program Design
front: Q099. How do elite sprinters differ in the Spring Mass Model?
back: They have higher stiffness and shorter ground contact times

title: Program Design
front: Q100. What are the training goals for improving running speed?
back: Develop high RFD, stiffness and SSC efficiency for rapid propulsive impulse

title: Program Design
front: Q101. List strength or power exercises that improve sprint speed.
back: Weightlifting derivatives such as cleans and snatch pulls

title: Program Design
front: Q102. Define complex training or PAP.
back: Alternating heavy resistance training and plyometrics to enhance neural output

title: Program Design
front: Q103. What are resisted sprint methods?
back: Sled towing or incline running with less than ten to twelve percent velocity loss or twenty to thirty percent body weight (except new research says 75% best!)

title: Program Design
front: Q104. What are assisted sprint methods?
back: Light towing or downhill running with less than ten percent assistance to improve stride rate

title: Program Design
front: Q105. List the four phases of the Speed Development Strategy.
back: Block one acceleration, Block two transition, Block three introduction to max speed, Block four max speed or endurance

title: Program Design
front: Q106. Give examples of drills for Block one acceleration.
back: Incline or sled sprints up to twenty meters

title: Program Design
front: Q107. Give examples of drills for Block two transition.
back: Push up starts or crouch sprints

title: Program Design
front: Q108. Give examples of drills for Block three introduction to max speed.
back: Fly in sprints thirty to sixty meters

title: Program Design
front: Q109. Give examples of drills for Block four max speed endurance.
back: Fly float fly or sixty to ninety meter repeats

title: Program Design
front: Q110. Define change of direction COD.
back: Explosive redirection of movement

title: Program Design
front: Q111. Define agility.
back: Change of direction combined with perceptual and cognitive reaction to a stimulus

title: Program Design
front: Q112. List physical determinants of COD and agility.
back: Eccentric strength braking ability, reacceleration power, trunk control, balance, decision speed

title: Program Design
front: Q113. List cognitive determinants of agility.
back: Visual scanning anticipation pattern recognition reaction accuracy

title: Program Design
front: Q114. What are typical ground contact times during agility drills?
back: Less than zero point three seconds

title: Program Design
front: Q115. List strength qualities contributing to agility.
back: Dynamic, Explosive Reactive, Eccentric, Multidirectional, Perceptual

title: Program Design
front: Q116. Give examples of dynamic strength exercises for agility.
back: Squats pulls lunges

title: Program Design
front: Q117. Give examples of explosive or reactive strength exercises for agility.
back: Box jumps jump squats sled pushes

title: Program Design
front: Q118. Give examples of eccentric strength drills for agility
back: Drop landings braking drills

title: Program Design
front: Q119. Give examples of perceptual agility drills.
back: Reactive cone drills small sided games

title: Program Design
front: Q120. List the four phases of the Agility Development Strategy.
back: Block one basic COD mechanics, Block two quick COD and reaccel, Block three high speed COD, Block four integrated reactive agility

title: Program Design
front: Q121. Give examples of Block two quick COD drills.
back: Z drills and angled cuts less than seventy five degrees

title: Program Design
front: Q122. Give examples of Block three high speed COD drills.
back: Cuts greater than seventy five degrees with reactive cues

title: Program Design
front: Q123. Give examples of Block four integrated reactive agility drills.
back: Small sided games and sport specific decision drills

title: Program Design
front: Q124. Define overload in aerobic training.
back: Progressively increase frequency, duration, or intensity beyond accustomed levels

title: Program Design
front: Q125. What happens when training frequency exceeds five sessions per week?
back: Injury risk increases

title: Program Design
front: Q126. What is the Karvonen formula for target heart rate?
back: Target HR equals resting HR plus percentage of heart rate reserve

title: Program Design
front: Q127. What is heart rate reserve (HRR)?
back: Maximum heart rate minus resting heart rate

title: Program Design
front: Q128. How does the %MHR method differ from the Karvonen method?
back: %MHR uses maximum heart rate only, Karvonen adds resting heart rate back in

title: Program Design
front: Q129. What is the relationship between intensity and duration?
back: Higher intensity means shorter duration and vice versa

title: Program Design
front: Q130. How much can frequency, intensity, or duration safely increase each week?
back: No more than ten percent

title: Program Design
front: Q131. List the five steps of program design in aerobic training.
back: Mode, Frequency, Intensity, Duration, Progression

title: Program Design
front: Q132. Define progression in aerobic training.
back: Gradual increase of frequency intensity or duration

title: Program Design
front: Q133. List the five major types of aerobic endurance training.
back: Long Slow Distance, Pace or Tempo, Interval, HIIT, Fartlek

title: Program Design
front: Q134. Describe Long Slow Distance training.
back: Low intensity about seventy percent VO2max for thirty to one hundred twenty minutes to build aerobic base

title: Program Design
front: Q135. Describe Fartlek training.
back: Alternating fast and slow periods for twenty to sixty minutes combining multiple systems

title: Program Design
front: Q136. What is the main purpose of HIIT?
back: Improve speed, running economy, and end of race performance

title: Program Design
front: Q137. Match each season to its aerobic goal.
back: Off season build base, Pre season improve VO2Max and LT, In season maintain and race, Post season active recovery

title: Program Design
front: Q138. What intensity and duration characterize Off season training?
back: Low to moderate intensity long duration

title: Program Design
front: Q139. What intensity and duration characterize Pre season aerobic training?
back: Moderate to high intensity moderate to long duration

title: Program Design
front: Q140. What intensity and duration characterize In season endurance training?
back: Low intensity + short for training high for races

title: Program Design
front: Q141. Define tapering.
back: Planned reduction of training VOLUME before competition; intensity and frequency are maintained

title: Program Design
front: Q142. List the three taper models.
back: Linear, Step, Progressive

title: Program Design
front: Q143. What is the typical duration of a taper period?
back: Seven to twenty eight days

title: Program Design
front: Q144. What is the definition of periodization?
back: Systematic variation of training variables such as volume, intensity, frequency, and exercise selection to maximize performance and prevent overtraining

title: Program Design
front: Q145. What is the main goal of periodization?
back: Sequence adaptations to build base, develop strength, peak, and recover

title: Program Design
front: Q146. List the three classic theoretical models of periodization (not linear etc!)
back: General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS), Stimulus Fatigue Recovery Adaptation (SFRA), Fitness Fatigue Paradigm

title: Program Design
front: Q147. In the GAS model what happens in the Alarm stage?
back: Fatigue and temporary performance decrease

title: Program Design
front: Q148. In the GAS model what happens in the Resistance stage?
back: Adaptation and performance improvement

title: Program Design
front: Q149. In the GAS model what happens in the Exhaustion stage?
back: Overtraining and performance decline

title: Program Design
front: Q150. In the SFRA model what determines recovery time?
back: Magnitude of fatigue from training load

title: Program Design
front: Q151. Which model views training as creating both fitness and fatigue effects?
back: Fitness Fatigue Paradigm

title: Program Design
front: Q152. In the Fitness Fatigue Paradigm which effect lasts longer?
back: Fitness

title: Program Design
front: Q153. In the Fitness Fatigue Paradigm which effect dissipates faster?
back: Fatigue

title: Program Design
front: Q154. What are the five structural levels of periodization?
back: Multiyear plan, Annual plan or macrocycle, Mesocycle, Microcycle, Training session

title: Program Design
front: Q155. How long does a mesocycle typically last?
back: Two to six weeks

title: Program Design
front: Q156. What is a microcycle?
back: A one week training block organizing daily variations

title: Program Design
front: Q157. What is an unloading week?
back: Every three to four weeks reduce total volume load by forty to sixty percent for recovery

title: Program Design
front: Q158. What are the four major training periods in a macrocycle?
back: Preparatory, First Transition, Competitive, Second Transition

title: Program Design
front: Q159. Which training period occurs during the off season?
back: Preparatory period

title: Program Design
front: Q160. Describe the Hypertrophy or Strength Endurance phase load reps and focus.
back: Fifty to seventy five percent one rep max, three to six sets of eight to twenty reps, develop muscular base and endurance

title: Program Design
front: Q161. Describe the Basic Strength phase load reps and focus.
back: Eighty to ninety five percent one rep max, two to six sets of two to six reps, increase maximal strength

title: Program Design
front: Q162. How does the Hypertrophy phase differ for strength vs endurance athletes?
back: Strength or power athletes focus on hypertrophy, endurance athletes focus on muscular endurance

title: Program Design
front: Q163. What is the purpose of the First Transition period?
back: Convert strength to power and increase sport specific velocity

title: Program Design
front: Q164. Describe the Strength or Power phase load reps and focus.
back: Thirty to ninety five percent one rep max, two to five sets of two to five reps, focus on explosive high velocity movement

title: Program Design
front: Q165. What are the two phases of the Competitive period?
back: Peaking and Maintenance

title: Program Design
front: Q166. Describe the Peaking phase load sets reps.
back: Fifty to greater than ninety three percent one rep max, one to three sets of one to three reps, optimize performance

title: Program Design
front: Q167. Describe the Maintenance phase load sets reps.
back: Eighty five to ninety three percent one rep max, two to five sets of three to six reps, maintain performance during season

title: Program Design
front: Q168. What is the focus of the Second Transition period?
back: Active rest recovery and mental restoration

title: Program Design
front: Q169. List intensity and volume trends across the four periods.
back: Preparatory low to moderate intensity high volume, First Transition intensity increases, Competitive high intensity low volume, Second Transition very low load

title: Program Design
front: Q170. What is the typical load range for Hypertrophy or Endurance work?
back: Fifty to seventy five percent one rep max

title: Program Design
front: Q171. What is the typical load range for Basic Strength work?
back: Eighty to ninety five percent one rep max

title: Program Design
front: Q172. What is the typical load range for Maintenance work?
back: Eighty five to ninety three percent one rep max

title: Program Design
front: Q173. What happens to volume load during an unloading week?
back: Reduced by forty to sixty percent

title: Program Design
front: Q174. Match each period to its seasonal timing.
back: Off season Preparatory, Pre season First Transition, In season Competitive, Post season Second Transition

title: Program Design
front: Q175. Fill in the blank The Preparatory period emphasizes ______ volume and ______ intensity.
back: High volume and low to moderate intensity

title: Program Design
front: Q176. Fill in the blank The Competitive period emphasizes ______ volume and ______ intensity.
back: Low volume and high intensity

title: Program Design
front: Q177. Which model increases intensity gradually across mesocycles?
back: Traditional Linear

title: Program Design
front: Q178. Which model changes reps and loads daily or weekly?
back: Undulating Nonlinear

title: Program Design
front: Q179. Give an example of a Traditional Linear load pattern (think HML)
back: Four by six at eighty five percent heavy, four by six at seventy five percent moderate, four by six at sixty five percent light

title: Program Design
front: Q180. Give an example of an Undulating Nonlinear pattern.
back: Tuesday four by six strength, Thursday three by ten hypertrophy, Saturday five by three power

title: Program Design
front: Q181. Fill in the blank Both linear and undulating models are ______ in practice.
back: Nonlinear

title: Program Design
front: Q182. Which model may reduce neural fatigue by varying loads daily?
back: Undulating Nonlinear

title: Program Design
front: Q183. Which model may limit peripheral fatigue due to lower weekly volume load?
back: Traditional Linear

title: Program Design
front: Q184. What should be scheduled every three to four weeks in either model?
back: Unloading microcycle

title: Program Design
front: Q185. What is the key takeaway comparing linear and undulating models?
back: Both effective, choice depends on athlete level goals and fatigue management

title: Program Design
front: Q186. Complex training: How should you pair and time heavy lifts with plyometrics to exploit PAP/PAPE?
back: Match patterns (e.g., squat → jump), then rest ~3-10 minutes before the explosive movement to express potentiation and boost power output.

title: Program Design
front: Q187. Force-vector specificity: Why emphasize horizontally loaded movements in acceleration training?
back: Horizontal loading (e.g., heavy sled pulls) transfers best to horizontal force production and acceleration; match loading vector to the task.

title: Program Design
front: Q188. Sled-pull loading: How do different sled loads shift adaptations per the sprint force-velocity profile?
back: Heavier loads (larger velocity decrement) preferentially increase force; lighter loads target velocity; all outperform unresisted sprints for short acceleration.

title: Program Design
front: Q189. Periodization: What weekly ordering within DUP can enhance strength gains?
back: A modified sequence such as Hypertrophy → Power → Strength can produce larger 1RM gains than a traditional configuration when volume is well-distributed.

title: Program Design
front: Q190. Exercise selection: What is performance modeling and how does it guide exercise choice?
back: Start from sport KPIs and needs analysis, diagnose constraints, then pick/regress/progress exercises to maximize transfer to those KPIs.

title: Program Design
front: Q191. Triathletes: How can strength training be integrated without harming endurance performance?
back: Program 2-3×/week, prioritize discipline‑specific patterns (hip/knee extension, trunk stiffness), and avoid interference near key endurance sessions.

title: Program Design
front: Q192. List 6 strengths (excl isometric) most load / slowest first
back: Absolute S, Accelerative S, Strength-speed (Olympic), Speed-strength, Explosive strength, Max speed (plyo)

title: Program Design
front: Q193. Depth jump
back: Step off a box, land on both feet, and immediately explode into a maximal jump with minimal ground contact time: quads and calves

title: Program Design
front: Q194. Squat jump
back: Start in a half-squat, pause, then jump straight up as high as possible and land softly before resetting: quads and glutes

title: Program Design
front: Q195. Countermovement jump
back: Stand tall, dip quickly into a shallow squat and rebound immediately into a maximal vertical jump: quads and glutes

title: Program Design
front: Q196. Pogo jumps
back: Perform a series of quick, low hops using stiff ankles and almost straight knees, bouncing rhythmically off the ground: calves and foot/ankle muscles

title: Program Design
front: Q197. Best way to increase first-step quickness
back: Increase stride rate (stride length increases naturally later)

title: Program Design
front: Q198. Sequence for athlete unable to do box jumps
back: Drop landings / drop freeze; depth jump to stick (light rebound); depth jump low; higher; single leg

title: Program Design
front: Q199. Bracketing technique
back: Less than and greater than normal resistance - acceleration training eg for shot put

title: Program Design
front: Q200. Rep ranges by training goal?
back: Strength ≤6 reps · Power 1-5 · Hypertrophy 6-12 · Muscular endurance ≥12

title: Program Design
front: Q201. Which does tapering reduce: D, F or I
back: D and F

title: Program Design
front: Q202. What training decreases GTO inhibitory response?
back: Plyo - trains nervous system to override inhibition

title: Program Design
front: Q203. What is neuromuscular training (3, 2)
back: Plyo + agility + strength to improve control and joint stability

title: Program Design
front: Q204. High cycling intensity produces (muscles)…
back: More hip and knee extensor contribution

title: Program Design
front: Q205. During sprint flight phase dorsiflexion or plantarflexion
back: Dorsiflexion (toe up)

title: Program Design
front: Q206. Higher intensity upper plyo: single arm throw, power drop, depth push up
back: Power drop

title: Program Design
front: Q207. Best way to improve max velocity sprinting
back: Practice max velocity sprinting

title: Program Design
front: Q208. Greatest impact on wide receiver max velocity - stride length or frequency
back: Stride freq

title: Program Design
front: Q209. Movement v physiological analysis
back: Movement patterns + muscular involvement; strength power hypertrophy endurance priorities

title: Program Design
front: Q210. Describe box jump
back: Jump onto a box; slowish SSC

title: Program Design
front: Q211. What is strength endurance + reps
back: Midway between strength and muscular endurance so 8-15 (similar to hypertrophy)

title: Program Design
front: Q212. Best slope for short distance sprinting over-speed training
back: 5.8 degrees

title: Program Design
front: Q213. Forearm position while running
back: Between waist and chest

title: Program Design
front: Q214. Picture a single leg box push off. What intensity?
back: Low

title: Program Design
front: Q215. Plyo high intensity lower body drills (1**+1+4)
back: Any single leg except box push off and ankle hop; any depth jump; cycled split squat jump; pike jump; double leg zig zag hop; 4 hurdle drill (SPZ4)

title: Program Design
front: Q216. Strength endurance reps and rest
back: 10 reps, 30 seconds

title: Program Design
front: Q217. Decel drill steps for half speed, 3/4 speed, full speed

title: Program Design
front: Q218. Cluster sets
back: Instead of 10 reps do 5x2 with 20s break

title: Program Design
front: Q219. Complex training how heavy
back: 85% or more 1RM

title: Program Design

title: Program Design
front: Q221. Recommended in-season training focus for a female cross-country runner?
back: Muscular endurance (circuits, ~60-70%, 12-20 reps) - reverse linear periodization for endurance athletes.

title: Program Design
front: Q222. Linear periodization phase with 4-5 sets, 2-5 reps, 87-95% 1RM?
back: First transition (late preseason). In-season drops to 1-3 sets.

title: Program Design
front: Q223. Linear periodization phase with high-volume lifting (3-6 sets, 8-20 reps)?
back: General preparatory (off-season) - highest volume, lowest intensity.

title: Program Design
front: Q224. During an aerobic base phase, what strength training does a XC runner do (reverse linear)?
back: Strength. Endurance athletes go strength off-season -> muscular endurance in-season.

title: Program Design
front: Q225. Which quality is programmed closest to competition in linear periodization?
back: Power - gains are transient and don't last long without training.

title: Program Design
front: Q226. Which is NOT recommended for youth athletes: depth jumps, 1RM testing, spinal loading?
back: Depth jumps / high-intensity plyometrics (contraindicated until growth plates close).

title: Program Design
front: Q227. Which has the shortest ground contact time: max-velocity sprint, acceleration, depth jump?
back: Max-velocity phase of sprinting (~0.1 s).

title: Program Design
front: Q228. What should a soccer player prioritize to maintain speed/agility late in a match?
back: Interval training (improves work capacity, lactate threshold, fatigued performance).

title: Program Design
front: Q229. Best CORE (primary) exercise for an off-season football lineman?
back: Tire flip - trains many movement patterns for GPP hypertrophy. (Crunch is accessory.)

title: Program Design
front: Q230. Best change-of-direction drill progression for novice athletes?
back: Z-cone drill (low velocity, <10 yd acceleration) - appropriate for beginners.

title: Program Design
front: Q231. Most advanced deceleration drill of the three?
back: Full speed, decelerate in 7 steps (progress half/3 -> 3/4/5 -> full/7).

title: Program Design
front: Q232. Approx reps at 83% 1RM on back squat?
back: ~7 reps.

title: Program Design
front: Q233. Baseball player's workout lacks what (DB press, lunges, bench, leg press, woodchop)?
back: Add a pulling exercise (cable low row) - no upper-back pull present.

title: Program Design
front: Q234. Which is NOT a recommended plyometric landing surface?
back: Hardwood floor. (Recommended: grass, rubber mat, suspended floor.)

title: Program Design
front: Q235. Volleyball player: 2-3x/wk, 3 months, 6-8 basic exercises, medium stress - training status?
back: Intermediate (training age 2-6 mo, 2-3x/wk, medium stress).

title: Program Design
front: Q236. Karvonen target heart rate formula?
back: Target HR = RHR + intensity% x (max HR - RHR).

title: Program Design
front: Q237. Older-adult resistance starting/progression prescription?
back: Start 1 set x 8-12 @ 40-50% 1RM; progress to 2-3 sets x 6-12 @ 70-85%.

title: Program Design
front: Q238. Older-adult power prescription?
back: 1-3 sets x 6-10 @ 40-60% 1RM at high velocity.

title: Program Design
front: Q246. Beginner load increments after the 2-for-2 rule?
back: Upper body +2.5-5 lb; lower body +5-10 lb.

title: Program Design
front: Q247. Plyometric foot contacts per session by level?
back: Beginner ~80-100; intermediate ~100-120; advanced ~120-200 contacts/session (low-intensity column).

title: Program Design

back: 16-42 in (typically 30-32 in); avoid boxes over 18 in if athlete is >220 lb.

back: 48-72 hr between sessions; 2-3x per week.

back: Change-of-direction ground contact time ~0.15-0.6 s (varies with angle of direction change).

title: Program Design
front: Q255. By what duration is an effort considered sprinting, and when is upright posture reached?
back: 15 s or less; upright posture by ~20 m.

title: Program Design
front: Q256. Pace/tempo training intensity and duration?
back: At lactate threshold (race pace), ~20-30 min.

title: Program Design
front: Q257. Interval training intensity and work:rest?
back: Near VO2max, work:rest 1:1.

title: Program Design
front: Q258. HIIT intensity and work:rest?
back: Greater than VO2max, work:rest 1:5.

title: Program Design

back: 3-5x per week.

title: Program Design
front: Q260. Max safe progression of a training variable per week?
back: <=5-10% per week.

title: Program Design
front: Q261. Typical taper duration?
back: 7-28 days.

title: Program Design
front: Q262. Length of a peaking window?
back: 7-14 days.

title: Program Design
front: Q263. Length of a microcycle?
back: 1-2 weeks.

title: Program Design
front: Q264. Length of a mesocycle?
back: Mesocycle: 2-6 weeks (4 weeks most common).

title: Program Design
front: Q265. Length of the second transition (active rest)?
back: 1-4 weeks.

title: Program Design
front: Q266. Power output at 90% 1RM vs 100% 1RM (bonus)?
back: Roughly double - lighter load plus much faster concentric speed.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q001. Olympic lift triple-extension order?
back: Plantar flexion → knee extension → hip extension → shrug → THEN bend elbows

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q002. Bench press points of contact?
back: 5 - both feet, hips, shoulders, head

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q003. Back squat spotting?
back: 2 spotters at the sides, hands under the bar; collars required

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q004. Deadlift/clean start: hips, knees, shoulders?
back: Hips above knees, below shoulders; shoulders over/slightly ahead of the bar

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q005. RAMP warm-up protocol?
back: Raise, Activate, Mobilize, Potentiate.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q006. Snatch grip width?
back: Wide - roughly fist-to-opposite-shoulder (or elbow-to-elbow with the bar at the hip).

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q007. Key technique for safe landings
back: Shoulders over knees, knees over toes, flex at hips knees and ankles

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q008. Why is landing technique critical? (V, D)
back: It reduces injury risk by controlling valgus stress and deceleration

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q009. What key coaching cue describes horizontal force application?
back: Push the ground away

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q010. Describe the basic sprint mechanics sequence.
back: Powerful extension through hips knees then ankles

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q011. At what distance is a sprinter nearly upright?
back: Around twenty meters

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q012. What characterizes the acceleration phase of sprinting?
back: Large backward vertical forces and short contact times about zero point zero nine seconds for elite athletes

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q013. What characterizes the maximal velocity phase?
back: Stacked alignment minimal vertical oscillation relaxed arms

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q014. What body position improves stability for COD?
back: Lower center of mass with hips behind plant foot

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q015. Describe proper braking and propulsion mechanics.
back: Decelerate under control then push the ground away for reacceleration

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q016. Why is trunk stability important for COD?
back: It allows efficient transfer of braking and propulsive forces

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q017. Deadlift variations: What distinguishes the trap/hex bar deadlift vs straight bar-and when is it advantageous?
back: More knee extensor demand and reduced lumbar moment; yields higher peak force/velocity/power at submax loads-useful when prioritizing power.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q018. Straight Arms Behind Back
back: How: Stand, clasp hands behind, lift arms. Muscles: ant delt, pec maj. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q019. Seated Lean-Back
back: How: Sit legs straight, hands behind, slide back. Muscles: delts, pec maj. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q020. Behind-Neck Stretch (Chicken Wing)
back: How: Arm overhead, pull elbow behind head. Muscles: triceps, lats. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q021. Cross Arm in Front of Chest
back: How: Pull arm across chest. Muscles: post delt, rhomboids. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q022. Arms Straight Up Above Head (Pillar)
back: How: Interlace fingers, reach up and back. Muscles: lats. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q023. Spinal Twist (Pretzel)
back: How: Twist torso using elbow on opposite knee. Muscles: obliques, erector spinae. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q024. Semi-Leg Straddle
back: How: Knees bent outward, lean forward. Muscles: erector spinae. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q025. Forward Lunge (Fencer)
back: How: Long step forward, sink hips. Muscles: hip flexors, RF. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q026. Supine Knee Flex
back: How: Pull one thigh to chest. Muscles: glut max, hams. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q027. Side Bend With Straight Arms
back: How: Arms overhead, lean sideways. Muscles: obliques, lats. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q028. Side Bend With Bent Arm
back: How: Elbow overhead, pull and lean sideways. Muscles: obliques, lats. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q029. Side Quadriceps Stretch
back: How: Lie on side, pull top ankle to butt. Muscles: quads, iliopsoas. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q030. Sitting Toe Touch
back: How: Reach for toes with legs straight. Muscles: hams, erector spinae. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q031. Semistraddle (Figure Four)
back: How: Bend one leg in, reach for straight leg. Muscles: hams, gastroc. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q032. Straddle (Spread Eagle)
back: How: Wide legs, reach side or center. Muscles: hams, hip add. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q033. Butterfly
back: How: Soles together, press knees down. Muscles: hip add. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q034. Wall Stretch (Calf)
back: How: Step back, heel down, lean forward. Muscles: gastroc, soleus. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q035. Step Stretch (Calf)
back: How: Lower heel off step. Muscles: gastroc, soleus. Type: S

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q036. Arm Swings
back: How: Swing arms across body while walking. Muscles: lats, delts. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q037. Inchworm
back: How: Walk hands to plank, then feet to hands. Muscles: erector spinae, hams. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q038. Lunge Walk
back: How: Step into deep lunge, alternate. Muscles: glut max, hams, quads. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q039. Lunge With Overhead Side Reach
back: How: Lunge forward, reach overhead and lean. Muscles: glut max, lats. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q040. Walking Knee Lift
back: How: Pull knee to chest while stepping. Muscles: glut max, hams. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q041. Forward Lunge With Elbow to Instep
back: How: Lunge, drop elbow to instep. Muscles: glut max, hams. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q042. Heel-to-Toe Walk
back: How: Heel strike, roll to toe. Muscles: gastroc, soleus. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q043. Walking Over and Under
back: How: Step over then duck under imaginary hurdles. Muscles: hip abd, hip add. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q044. Inverted Hamstring Stretch
back: How: Single-leg hinge, reach forward. Muscles: glut max, hams. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q045. Straight-Leg March
back: How: Kick straight leg up as you march. Muscles: hams, hip flexors. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q046. Spiderman Crawl
back: How: Crawl forward, knee outside elbow. Muscles: glut max, hams, obliques. Type: D

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q047. What is the primary purpose of a warm-up?
back: Prepare athlete mentally and physically and help reduce injury risk.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q048. What are two temperature-related effects of a warm-up?
back: Increased muscle/core temperature and improved neural function.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q049. What are two non-temperature-related effects of a warm-up?
back: Increased blood flow and increased oxygen consumption.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q050. How long should a full warm-up typically last?
back: 10-20 minutes.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q051. How close to activity should the warm-up finish?
back: Within 15 minutes.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q052. What does the Raise phase of RAMP accomplish?
back: Elevates HR, temperature, blood flow, and begins skill preparation.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q053. What happens in the Activate & Mobilize phase of RAMP? Eg X and Y to improve P and Q
back: Dynamic mobility through patterns like squat and lunge to improve ROM and control.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q054. What is the goal of the Potentiate phase of RAMP?
back: Increase intensity to match the session and prepare for speed/power.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q055. Define flexibility.
back: Range of motion at a joint.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q056. Define mobility (1 + 3)
back: ROM with control including strength, coordination, and balance.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q057. Why is optimal ROM more important than maximal ROM?
back: Sport requires specific ROM and too much or too little increases injury risk.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q058. How often should stretching be performed to improve ROM?
back: At least 2 times per week.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q059. How long should a static stretch be held?
back: 15-30 seconds.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q060. When is stretching most effective for increasing ROM?
back: After practice when muscles are warm.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q061. What should always precede stretching?
back: Light general warm-up to raise muscle temperature.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q062. How long is the initial passive stretch in PNF techniques?
back: 10 seconds.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q063. Describe the Contract-Relax PNF sequence.
back: 10s passive stretch → concentric contraction of target → 30s passive stretch.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q064. Why is Hold-Relax with Agonist Contraction most effective?
back: Uses autogenic and reciprocal inhibition - autogenic means antag (target) contracts before; recip means agonist contracts simultaneously .

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q065. What type of stretching is preferred in warm-ups?
back: Dynamic stretching.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q066. What type of stretching is preferred after practice?
back: Static or PNF.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q067. What is the sticking point?
back: The portion of the concentric phase where the lift slows and is hardest, usually just after the eccentric-concentric transition.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q068. List the five handgrip types used in resistance training.
back: Pronated, supinated, neutral, alternated, hook grip.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q069. What is a pronated grip?
back: Palms down.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q070. What is a supinated grip?
back: Palms up.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q071. What is a neutral grip?
back: Knuckles lateral (handshake position).

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q072. What is an alternated grip?
back: One pronated and one supinated.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q073. What is a hook grip?
back: Thumb trapped under fingers for stronger hold.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q074. List the three basic grip widths.
back: Common, narrow, wide (fist to opp shoulder; elbow to elbow)

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q075. Describe the clean grip.
back: Slightly wider than shoulder-width.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q076. Describe the snatch grip.
back: Very wide grip based on shoulder-to-fist or elbow-to-elbow method.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q077. Describe proper standing lower-body positioning for exercises.
back: Feet slightly wider than hip-width with heels and balls of feet on the floor.

title: Exercise Technique

title: Exercise Technique

back: To align joints with the machine’s axis for safety and proper loading.

title: Exercise Technique

back: Through the sticking point (the most strenuous part).

back: During the easier eccentric phase.

back: To increase torso rigidity for spinal support during heavy structural lifts.

back: For trained lifters handling heavy structural exercises.

back: Stand close, maintain neutral spine, stable stance.

back: A power rack with safety bars.

back: Alternated grip.

title: Exercise Technique

back: Near the athlete’s wrists or forearms.

title: Exercise Technique

back: Only when the load exceeds one spotter’s safe capability.

back: Liftoff cues, reps, readiness, and need for help.

back: Assist the athlete in moving the bar from supports into start position.

back: One spotter lifts off, both assist with re-racking.

back: Only enough to assist past the sticking point.

title: Exercise Technique

back: Until the bar is fully re-racked or safely on the floor.

title: Exercise Technique

back: Learn to safely drop or abandon the bar forward or backward.

title: Exercise Technique

back: Proper alignment for safe loading of joints and muscles.

title: Exercise Technique
front: Q098. What should be established before lifting any significant load?
back: Grip, posture, and torso stability.

title: Exercise Technique

back: Inter-rater reliability

front: Q003. Reactive Strength Index = ?
back: Jump height ÷ ground-contact time (drop jump)

title: Program Implementation
front: Q004. Overtraining continuum?
back: Acute fatigue → functional overreaching → non-functional overreaching → overtraining syndrome

title: Program Implementation
front: Q005. Functional vs non-functional overreaching?
back: FOR → supercompensation after a deload; NFOR → only returns to baseline / prolonged

title: Program Implementation
front: Q006. Sympathetic vs parasympathetic overtraining?
back: Sympathetic: power/strength athletes, ↑ resting HR. Parasympathetic: endurance, ↓ resting HR, more advanced

title: Program Implementation
front: Q007. Test order to avoid fatigue contamination?
back: Non-fatiguing first: agility / power / max-strength → anaerobic-capacity → aerobic-capacity LAST.

title: Program Implementation
front: Q008. Validity vs reliability?
back: Validity = measures what it claims. Reliability = consistent/repeatable. A valid test must be reliable.

title: Program Implementation
front: Q009. Margaria-Kalamen test measures?
back: Anaerobic power (a stair-climb power test).

title: Program Implementation
front: Q010. Tissue healing phases (rehab)?
back: Inflammation → repair/proliferation → remodeling/maturation.

title: Program Implementation
front: Q011. Sprain vs strain?
back: Sprain = LIGAMENT injury; Strain = MUSCLE/tendon injury. Both graded I-III.

title: Program Implementation
front: Q012. Dislocation vs subluxation?
back: Dislocation = complete joint displacement; subluxation = partial.

title: Program Implementation
front: Q013. Tissue healing phases + collagen?
back: Inflammatory (2-7 d) → Fibroblastic repair (Type III collagen, weak; 2 d-2 mo) → Maturation/remodeling (Type I collagen, stronger; months-yrs).

title: Program Implementation
front: Q014. DeLorme vs Oxford rehab loading?
back: DeLorme = progressive (50→75→100% of 10RM); Oxford = regressive (100→75→50%).

title: Program Implementation
front: Q015. Strongest predictor of future injury?
back: Previous injury.

title: Program Implementation
front: Q016. Sports-medicine team roles?
back: Physician = diagnosis; AT/PT = rehab; CSCS = reconditioning; RD / physiologist / psych = support.

title: Program Implementation
front: Q017. Macrotrauma vs microtrauma?
back: Macrotrauma = single acute overload (sprain, fracture, contusion); microtrauma = repetitive overuse (stress fracture, tendinopathy).

title: Program Implementation
front: Q018. Injury-prevention programs / eccentric training?
back: Sportsmetrics & PEP improve landing mechanics → ↓ ACL/ankle injuries; eccentric training ↓ hamstring injuries.

title: Program Implementation

back: Daily Adjustable Progressive Resistance Exercise - autoregulated; reps achieved on a set set the next load.
